quiz: Think about one physical chair that is sold again for every show. Status must belong to the thing that changes per show.
Nothing is stuck waiting and nothing leaks. Both threads simply read the old value before either writes. Which bug family is that?
Ask whether a booking for one show should ever need to wait for a booking on a totally different show.
Correctness should not depend on a background job running on time. What does a hold time in the past really mean?
A deadlock needs a cycle of waiting. Ask what simple rule, applied by every thread, makes it impossible for two of them to wait on each other.
Use whole paise, not decimals. The parts must add back to exactly 10000 paise, so the leftover paise must go somewhere.
Only the other two people owe money to the payer. Work out each share and who owes whom.
Each transfer settles at least one person fully. Count how many transfers that allows for n people.
Finding the true minimum number of transfers is a hard search problem. Does a simple greedy rule always find it?
One title can have many physical copies, each with its own status and barcode. Which class holds what?
Think of a fair queue: who gets first claim on a returned copy, and is it held for them or put back on the shelf?
Think Open/Closed: closed for modification, open for extension. Which option adds behaviour without touching existing checkout code?
The seats now belong to someone else. Never take them back; think about what you owe the paying user instead.
interview: Cover clarifying requirements, listing core entities, the booking flow, and where concurrency and holds fit in, before writing code.
Explain that seat status changes per show, so you need a class for one seat inside one show, and what breaks without it.
Discuss making check and write atomic: locks, compare-and-set, or a conditional database update, and the lock scope you choose.
Mention lazy expiry checked on every read, an optional sweeper for cleanup, and why correctness must not depend on the sweeper.
Cover re-checking under the lock that the hold is still yours and alive, never stealing seats, refunding idempotently, and reducing the case.
Cover users, groups, expenses, splits, and a balance map per pair or net per user, plus why you store money as integers.
Explain floating point rounding errors and suggest integer minor units like paise or a decimal type, with a rounding rule.
Explain netting each person's balance, then greedy matching of debtors and creditors, the transfer bound, and that it is not always optimal.
Mention a split strategy interface so a new split type is a new class, plus validation that parts add up to the total.
Walk the happy path, then failures: no free copy, member limit, unpaid fines, reference-only books, and how each is reported.
Cover a waitlist per title, holding the returned copy for the first person, notification, and a hold expiry that moves to the next.
Suggest a fine policy or strategy object chosen per member or book type, so rules change without editing checkout code.
Name Strategy, Observer, State, Facade, Decorator and rule chains, and point to where each appears in booking, Splitwise and the library.
Mention many threads racing for the same seats, asserting no double booking, repeating runs, and injecting a fake clock.
Explain that in-memory locks stop working across servers, so move the atomic check to the database or a shared store like Redis.
